stem.text: Each part of this question gives a series whose terms are defined for all integers \( n \ge 1 \). In each part, use the limit comparison test with the comparison series named in that part.

parts.prompt: Determine whether the series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2n + 1}{n^{3} + 4} \) converges or diverges, using the series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{2}} \). Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: The limit is positive and finite and the sum of 1/n^2 is a convergent p-series (p = 2 > 1), so the given series converges.

points.criterion: Forms the quotient of the general terms, ((2n + 1)/(n^3 + 4))/(1/n^2) = (2n^3 + n^2)/(n^3 + 4), or the reciprocal quotient.
Writes the limit of the quotient with limit notation and evaluates it as 2, or as 1/2 for the reciprocal quotient.

States that the limit is positive and finite and that the sum of 1/n^2 converges as a p-series with p = 2 > 1, and concludes that the series of (2n + 1)/(n^3 + 4) converges; comparing the limit with 1 does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Determine whether the series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sin\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) \) converges or diverges, using the harmonic series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n} \). Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: For n >= 1, 0 < 1/n <= 1 < pi, so every term is positive. Form the quotient.
With u = 1/n, u approaches 0 as n grows.
The limit is positive and finite and the harmonic series diverges, so the given series diverges.

points.criterion: Forms the quotient sin(1/n)/(1/n), or its reciprocal (1/n)/sin(1/n).
Writes the limit of the quotient with limit notation and evaluates it as 1, for example through the limit of sin(u)/u as u approaches 0.
States that the limit is positive and finite and that the harmonic series diverges, and concludes that the series of sin(1/n) diverges.

parts.prompt: Show that the series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n}\sqrt{n}}{n^{2} + 1} \) converges absolutely, using the series \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{3/2}} \).

worked_solution.text: Quotient of the absolute value of the general term and the comparison term.
The limit is positive and finite and the sum of 1/n^(3/2) is a convergent p-series (p = 3/2 > 1), so the series of absolute values converges and the given series converges absolutely.

points.criterion: Forms the quotient of the absolute value of the general term, sqrt(n)/(n^2 + 1), and 1/n^(3/2), equal to n^2/(n^2 + 1), or the reciprocal quotient; a quotient built on the signed term (-1)^n sqrt(n)/(n^2 + 1) does not earn the point.
Writes the limit of the quotient with limit notation and evaluates it as 1.

States that the limit is positive and finite and that the sum of 1/n^(3/2) converges as a p-series with p = 3/2 > 1, and concludes that the series of absolute values converges, so the given series converges absolutely.
